Shebaniah
sheb-a-nī'ä
n. (a Levite who stood upon the stairs and cried with a loud voice unto the LORD in the great confession of Nehemiah 9; also a priest who blew with the trumpets before the ark)
From Hebrew Shebanyah, understood as the LORD hath grown him up or increased by the LORD, from a root meaning to grow, with Yah. Several men of the name serve in the restoration, all of them Levites or priests.

Biblical Definition

Shebaniah belongs to the twenty-fourth day of the seventh month, the day of the great confession, when the children of Israel assembled with fasting and with sackcloth and earth upon them, separated themselves from strangers, and stood and confessed their sins and the iniquities of their fathers for a fourth part of the day, and read in the book of the law for another fourth part. Two lists of Levites are given, and he is in both: “Then stood up upon the stairs, of the Levites, Jeshua, and Bani, Kadmiel, Shebaniah, Bunni, Sherebiah, Bani, and Chenani, and cried with a loud voice unto the LORD their God” (Neh 9:4), and then in the summons to praise: “Then the Levites, Jeshua, and Kadmiel, Bani, Hashabniah, Sherebiah, Hodijah, Shebaniah, and Pethahiah, said, Stand up and bless the LORD your God for ever and ever: and blessed be thy glorious name, which is exalted above all blessing and praise” (Neh 9:5). What follows is the longest prayer in the Old Testament, a recital of the whole history of God's dealing with Israel from Abram to that morning, ending in a sealed covenant. He is named again among the Levites who set their seal (Neh 10:12), and a priest of the name blew with the trumpets before the ark in David's day (1Ch 15:24).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) has no article for Shebaniah; in sacred history he is a Levite who led the confession and the blessing in the days of Nehemiah.

SHEBANIAH, n. The LORD hath increased him; a proper name borne by Levites and priests.

A Levite who stood upon the stairs and cried with a loud voice unto the LORD.

He was among those who called the people to stand up and bless the LORD their God.

He set his seal to the covenant which the Levites made in the days of Nehemiah.

A priest of the name blew with the trumpets before the ark of God in the days of David.

Key Scripture

Neh 9:4 — "Then stood up upon the stairs, of the Levites, Jeshua, and Bani, Kadmiel, Shebaniah, Bunni, Sherebiah, Bani, and Chenani, and cried with a loud voice unto the LORD their God."

Neh 9:5 — "Then the Levites, Jeshua, and Kadmiel, Bani, Hashabniah, Sherebiah, Hodijah, Shebaniah, and Pethahiah, said, Stand up and bless the LORD your God for ever and ever: and blessed be thy glorious name, which is exalted above all blessing and praise."

Neh 10:12 — "Zaccur, Sherebiah, Shebaniah,"

Neh 12:14 — "Of Melicu, Jonathan; of Shebaniah, Joseph;"

Modern Corruption

Corporate confession of the sins of the fathers is now dismissed as unjust inherited guilt, or else replaced with the ritual apologies of identity politics. Scripture teaches genuine covenant solidarity, and Nehemiah 9 shows what real confession looks like — addressed to God, resting on His character, and ending in obedience.

expand to see more

Two errors stand on either side of this chapter. The first says that no man can confess another's sin, that guilt is strictly individual, and that the Levites were indulging a primitive notion of inherited blame. The second, now common in the churches, borrows the form of Nehemiah 9 for the categories of modern grievance politics — corporate lament liturgies, generational apologies to demographic groups, penance offered horizontally to men rather than vertically to God, with no absolution possible because none is on offer. Both miss what the chapter does. Israel confesses to God, and the confession is answered by a covenant.

Scripture does hold real covenant solidarity: Daniel prays “We have sinned, and have committed iniquity, and have done wickedly, and have rebelled, even by departing from thy precepts and from thy judgments” (Dan 9:5), including himself in a guilt he had not personally incurred, and God commanded Israel to confess “their iniquity, and the iniquity of their fathers” (Lev 26:40). But Scripture equally holds personal accountability: “The son shall not bear the iniquity of the father, neither shall the father bear the iniquity of the son” (Eze 18:20). The two are not in competition; the covenant community owns the sins of its history before God, and each man answers for his own. What makes Nehemiah 9 different from every modern imitation is its object and its end: it is spoken to a God whose glorious name is exalted above all blessing and praise, and it finishes not in perpetual lament but in a written covenant to obey.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew Shebanyah (H7645), Shebaniah; yadah (H3034), to confess, give thanks; barak (H1288), to bless; 'amanah (H548), a sure covenant, a written agreement; ma'alah (H4609), stairs, steps.

expand to see more

Hebrew Shebanyah (H7645) — Shebaniah; a Levite of the restoration.

Hebrew yadah (H3034) — to confess and to give thanks, one verb for both.

Hebrew barak (H1288) — to bless; ‘stand up and bless the LORD’.

Hebrew 'amanah (H548) — a sure covenant; the sealed writing of Nehemiah 9:38.

Hebrew ma'alah (H4609) — stairs; where the Levites stood to cry.

Usage

"“Cried with a loud voice unto the LORD their God” — confession that was not quiet."

"“Stand up and bless the LORD your God for ever and ever” — the summons before the longest prayer."

"“Which is exalted above all blessing and praise” — the ground of the whole chapter."
